claims.text: The untreated starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
A controlled amount of coherent nanoprecipitates can be introduced as the intervention.
A controlled amount of nanotwins can alternatively be introduced as the intervention.
Coherent nanoprecipitates or nanotwins will improve the alloy's room-temperature tensile ductility.
Coherent nanoprecipitates or nanotwins will retain or increase the alloy's strength.
The predicted outcome is an increase in tensile strength rather than merely strength retention.
Coherent twin boundaries accommodate dislocations through interactions such as transmission and boundary-parallel motion.
Dislocation accommodation at coherent boundaries causes simultaneous increases in strength and ductility.
The intervention is intended to operate under room-temperature tensile testing and service conditions.
The optimal amount and spatial distribution of nanoprecipitates or nanotwins are uncertain.
The hypothesis is falsified if a treated specimen does not show both improved tensile ductility and improved tensile strength relative to an untreated specimen.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis permits retained strength as a successful result, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule require strength to improve. A treatment that improves ductility while retaining unchanged strength would satisfy the hypothesis but be classified as falsifying it.
